{{Short description|Order type of the set of all recursive ordinals}}
{{more footnotes needed|date=September 2021}}

In mathematics, particularly [[set theory]], '''non-recursive ordinals''' are [[large countable ordinal]]s greater than all the [[recursive ordinal]]s, and therefore can not be expressed using [[Ordinal notation|recursive ordinal notation]]s.

== The Church–Kleene ordinal and variants ==
The smallest non-recursive ordinal is the '''Church–Kleene ordinal''', <math>\omega_1^{\mathsf{CK}}</math>, named after [[Alonzo Church]] and [[S. C. Kleene]]; its [[order type]] is the set of all [[recursive ordinal]]s. Since the successor of a recursive ordinal is recursive, the Church–Kleene ordinal is a [[limit ordinal]]. It is also the smallest ordinal that is not [[Hyperarithmetical theory|hyperarithmetical]], and the smallest [[admissible ordinal]] after <math>\omega</math> (an ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called admissible if <math>L_\alpha \models \mathsf{KP}</math>.) The <math>\omega_1^{\mathsf{CK}}</math>-recursive subsets of <math>\omega</math> are exactly the <math>\Delta^1_1</math> subsets of <math>\omega</math>.<ref name="Zoo">D. Madore, [http://www.madore.org/~david/math/ordinal-zoo.pdf A Zoo of Ordinals] (2017). Accessed September 2021.</ref>

The notation <math>\omega_1^{\mathsf{CK}}</math> is in reference to <math>\omega_1</math>, the [[first uncountable ordinal]], which is the set of all countable ordinals, analogously to how the Church–Kleene ordinal is the set of all recursive ordinals. Some old sources use <math>\omega_1</math> to denote the Church–Kleene ordinal.<ref name="RichterAczel73">W. Richter, P. Aczel, [https://www.duo.uio.no/handle/10852/44063 Inductive Definitions and Reflecting Properties of Admissible Ordinals] (1973, p.15). Accessed 2021 October 28.</ref>

For a set <math>x\subseteq\mathbb N</math>, a set is <math>x</math>-computable if it is computable from a [[Turing machine]] with an [[oracle machine|oracle]] that queries <math>x</math>. The relativized Church–Kleene ordinal <math>\omega_1^x</math> is the [[Infimum and supremum|supremum]] of the order types of <math>x</math>-computable relations. The Friedman–Jensen–Sacks theorem states that for every countable admissible ordinal <math>\alpha</math>, there exists a set <math>x</math> such that <math>\alpha=\omega_1^x</math>.<ref>{{citation
| last1=Sacks | first1=Gerald E.|author1link = Gerald Sacks| title=Countable admissible ordinals and hyperdegrees
| date=1976
| journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]]
| volume=19
| issue=2
| pages=213–262
| doi=10.1016/0001-8708(76)90187-0 | doi-access=free}}</ref>

<math>\omega_\omega^{\mathsf{CK}}</math>, first defined by [[Stephen G. Simpson]]{{citation needed|date=May 2023}} is an extension of the Church–Kleene ordinal. This is the smallest limit of admissible ordinals, yet this ordinal is not admissible. Alternatively, this is the smallest <math>\alpha</math> such that <math>L_\alpha \cap \mathsf{P}(\omega)</math> is a model of [[Second-order arithmetic|<math>\Pi^1_1</math>-comprehension]].<ref name="Zoo">D. Madore, [http://www.madore.org/~david/math/ordinal-zoo.pdf A Zoo of Ordinals] (2017). Accessed September 2021.</ref>

== Recursively [X] ordinals ==
The <math>\alpha</math>th admissible ordinal is sometimes denoted by <math>\tau_\alpha</math>.<ref>P. G. Hinman, ''Recursion-Theoretic Hierarchies'' (1978), pp.419--420. Perspectives in Mathematical Logic, ISBN 3-540-07904-1.</ref><ref name="Barwise76">[[John Barwise|J. Barwise]], ''Admissible Sets and Structures'' (1976), pp.174--176. Perspectives in Logic, Cambridge University Press, ISBN 3-540-07451-1.</ref>

Recursively [X] ordinals, where [X] typically represents a [[large cardinal]] property, are kinds of nonrecursive ordinals.<ref name="Rathjen93">{{citation
| last1=Rathjen | first1=Michael
| title=Proof theory of reflection
| journal=[[Annals of Pure and Applied Logic]]
| volume=68
| issue=2
| date=1994
| pages=181–224
| doi=10.1016/0168-0072(94)90074-4 | doi-access=free
| url=https://www1.maths.leeds.ac.uk/~rathjen/Ehab.pdf}}</ref> Rathjen has called these ordinals the "recursively large counterparts" of X,<ref>M. Rathjen, "The Realm of Ordinal Analysis" (2006). [https://web.archive.org/web/20231207051454/https://www1.maths.leeds.ac.uk/~rathjen/realm.pdf Archived] 7 December 2023.</ref> however the use of "recursively large" here is not to be confused with the notion of an ordinal being recursive.

An ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called ''recursively inaccessible'' if it is admissible and a limit of admissibles. Alternatively, <math>\alpha</math> is recursively inaccessible iff <math>\alpha</math> is the <math>\alpha</math>th admissible ordinal,<ref name="Barwise76" /> or iff <math>L_\alpha \models \mathsf{KPi}</math>, an extension of [[Kripke–Platek set theory]] stating that each set is contained in a model of Kripke–Platek set theory. Under the condition that <math>L_\alpha\vDash\textrm{V=HC}</math> ("every set is [[Hereditary property|hereditarily countable]]"), <math>\alpha</math> is recursively inaccessible iff <math>L_\alpha \cap \mathsf{P}(\omega)</math> is a model of [[Second-order arithmetic|<math>\Delta^1_2</math>-comprehension]].<ref>W. Marek, [http://matwbn.icm.edu.pl/ksiazki/fm/fm101/fm101120.pdf Some comments on the paper by Artigue, Isambert, Perrin, and Zalc] (1976), ICM. Accessed 19 May 2023.</ref>

An ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called ''recursively hyperinaccessible'' if it is recursively inaccessible and a limit of recursively inaccessibles, or where <math>\alpha</math> is the <math>\alpha</math>th recursively inaccessible. Like "hyper-inaccessible cardinal", different authors conflict on this terminology.

An ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called ''recursively Mahlo'' if it is admissible and for any <math>\alpha</math>-recursive function <math>f : \alpha \rightarrow \alpha</math> there is an admissible <math>\beta < \alpha</math> such that <math>\left\{f(\gamma)\mid\gamma\in\beta\right\}\subseteq\beta</math> (that is, <math>\beta</math> is closed under <math>f</math>).<ref name="RichterAczel73" /> Mirroring the [[Mahlo cardinal|Mahloness hierarchy]], <math>\alpha</math> is ''recursively <math>\gamma</math>-Mahlo'' for an ordinal <math>\gamma</math> if it is admissible and for any <math>\alpha</math>-recursive function <math>f : \alpha \rightarrow \alpha</math> there is an admissible ordinal <math>\beta < \alpha</math> such that <math>\beta</math> is closed under <math>f</math>, and <math>\beta</math> is recursively <math>\delta</math>-Mahlo for all <math>\delta<\gamma</math>.<ref name="Rathjen93" />

An ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called ''recursively weakly compact'' if it is <math>\Pi_3</math>-reflecting, or equivalently,<ref name="RichterAczel73" /> 2-admissible. These ordinals have strong recursive Mahloness properties, if α is  <math>\Pi_3</math>-reflecting then <math>\alpha</math> is recursively <math>\alpha</math>-Mahlo.<ref name="Rathjen93" />

== Weakenings of stable ordinals ==
An ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is stable if <math>L_\alpha</math> is a <math>\Sigma_1</math>-[[Elementary substructure|elementary-substructure]] of <math>L</math>, denoted <math>L_\alpha\preceq_1 L</math>.<ref>J. Barwise, ''Admissible Sets and Structures'' (1976), Cambridge University Press, Perspectives in Logic.</ref> These are some of the largest named nonrecursive ordinals appearing in a model-theoretic context, for instance greater than <math>\min\{\alpha: L_\alpha \models T\}</math> for any computably axiomatizable theory <math>T</math>.<ref>W. Marek, K. Rasmussen, {{WorldCat|oclc=1280819208|name=Spectrum of L}} ([https://eudml.org/doc/268487 EuDML] page), Państwowe Wydawn. Accessed 2022-12-01.</ref><sup>Proposition 0.7</sup>. There are various weakenings of stable ordinals:<ref name="Zoo" />

* A countable ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called <math>(+1)</math>-stable [[If and only if|iff]] <math>L_\alpha \preceq_1 L_{\alpha+1}</math>. 
** The smallest <math>(+1)</math>-stable ordinal is much larger than the smallest recursively weakly compact ordinal: it has been shown that the smallest <math>(+1)</math>-stable ordinal is <math>\Pi_n</math>-reflecting for all finite <math>n</math>.<ref name="RichterAczel73" />
** In general, a countable ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called <math>(+\beta)</math>-stable iff <math>L_\alpha \preceq_1 L_{\alpha+\beta}</math>.
* A countable ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called <math>(^+)</math>-stable iff <math>L_\alpha \preceq_1 L_{\alpha^+}</math>, where <math>\alpha^+</math> is the smallest admissible ordinal <math>> \alpha</math>. The smallest <math>(^+)</math>-stable ordinal is again much larger than the smallest <math>(+1)</math>-stable or the smallest <math>(+\beta)</math>-stable for any constant <math>\beta</math>.
* A countable ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called <math>(^{++})</math>-stable iff <math>L_\alpha \preceq_1 L_{\alpha^{++}}</math>, where <math>\alpha^+</math> and <math>\alpha^{++}</math> are the two smallest admissible ordinals <math>> \alpha</math>. The smallest <math>(^{++})</math>-stable ordinal is larger than the smallest <math>\Sigma^1_1</math>-reflecting.
* A countable ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called inaccessibly-stable iff <math>L_\alpha \preceq_1 L_{\beta}</math>, where <math>\beta</math> is the smallest recursively inaccessible ordinal <math>> \alpha</math>. The smallest inaccessibly-stable ordinal is larger than the smallest <math>(^{++})</math>-stable.
* A countable ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called Mahlo-stable iff <math>L_\alpha \preceq_1 L_{\beta}</math>, where <math>\beta</math> is the smallest recursively Mahlo ordinal <math>> \alpha</math>. The smallest Mahlo-stable ordinal is larger than the smallest inaccessibly-stable.
* A countable ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called doubly <math>(+1)</math>-stable iff <math>L_\alpha \preceq_1 L_{\beta} \preceq_1 L_{\beta+1}</math>. The smallest doubly <math>(+1)</math>-stable ordinal is larger than the smallest Mahlo-stable.

== Larger nonrecursive ordinals ==
Even larger nonrecursive ordinals include:<ref name="Zoo" />
* The least ordinal <math>\alpha</math> such that <math>L_\alpha \preceq_1 L_\beta</math> where <math>\beta</math> is the smallest nonprojectible ordinal.
* An ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is nonprojectible if <math>\alpha</math> is a limit of ''<math>\alpha</math>''-stable ordinals, or; if the set <math>X = \left\{ \beta < \alpha \mid L_\beta \preceq_1 L_\alpha\right\}</math> is unbounded in ''<math>\alpha</math>''.
* The ordinal of ramified analysis, often written as <math>\beta_0</math>. This is the smallest <math>\beta</math> such that <math>L_\beta \cap \mathsf{P}(\omega)</math> is a model of [[Second-order arithmetic|second-order comprehension]], or <math>L_\beta \models \mathsf{ZFC^{-}}</math>, which is <math>\mathsf{ZFC}</math> without the [[axiom of power set]].
* The least ordinal <math>\alpha</math> such that <math>L_\alpha \models \mathsf{KP} + \text{'}\omega_1\text{ exists'}</math>. This ordinal has been characterized by Toshiyasu Arai.<ref>T. Arai, [https://arxiv.org/abs/1102.0596 A Sneak Preview of Proof Theory of Ordinals] (1997, p.17). Accessed 2021 October 28.</ref>
* The least ordinal <math>\alpha</math> such that <math>L_\alpha \models \mathsf{ZFC^{-}} + \text{'}\omega_1\text{ exists'}</math>.
* The least stable ordinal.
